meta: Plums from Pomona Britannica, George Brookshaw's 1806 aquatint of fruit grown in the gardens of Hampton Court Palace.
about: Plums fill this plate from Pomona Britannica, a book of fruit grown in the gardens at Hampton Court Palace. Those gardens were the most famous around London. The book set out to show the finest varieties grown in England. George Brookshaw made the plate in 1806, and the Cleveland Museum of Art notes that most of the 90 plates in the large book have dark aquatint backgrounds, as this one does.

meta: Two girls caught mid-dance lesson in Cecilia Beaux's 1898 double portrait Dorothea and Francesca, at the Art Institute of Chicago.
about: Two sisters move together in a dancing lesson. Cecilia Beaux painted them in 1898, and the Art Institute of Chicago says the picture cares more about their matching movement than about who each girl was. They were the daughters of her friends Helena de Kay and Richard Watson Gilder, a well-known couple in New York. The museum reads the scene as a step from girlhood toward adolescence. Beaux won portrait commissions in a market run by men, and she later became the first woman on the faculty of the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.

meta: Musical instruments in soft window light, with no one to play them: Vilhelm Hammershøi's 1907 Interior. The Music Room, Strandgade 30.
about: Hammershøi lived in a Copenhagen apartment at Strandgade 30 for eleven years and painted its rooms again and again. Here a few musical instruments sit in soft light from a window we can't see. Nobody is playing, and the Art Institute of Chicago says the room feels silent. The museum describes the apartment as a stage set for him, with furniture moved around for how it looked, not how it was used. Rilke wrote that his work is long and slow. Look at the small, flickering brushstrokes.

meta: The racehorse Lexington in a portrait by Thomas J. Scott, who painted him in Kentucky in the 1850s.
about: Lexington was born in Kentucky in 1850 and sired more winning horses than any other American thoroughbred. Thomas J. Scott painted him while living in Kentucky, when the horse was at his peak. Scott also wrote about him for Turf, Field and Farm. He said Lexington was without a peer, very wide across the shoulders and with no surplus ounce on him. The Smithsonian American Art Museum points to the tones in the painting, which bring out the glossy coat and the lean frame.

meta: A huge churning wave on the Maine coast: Winslow Homer's 1887 watercolor Prout's Neck, Breaking Wave.
about: Winslow Homer fished from this spot near Cannon Rock almost every day in summer and fall, so he had watched waves like this a thousand times. That is the account of the Art Institute of Chicago, which cites the scholar Philip Beam. Homer marked out the white foam with resist, probably chalk, then built up the textures of water, rock and sky by layering and scraping the paint. He also blotted and rewetted it. The museum says the picture was carefully planned, though it feels vigorous and immediate.

meta: Golden light over trees and fields in October, John Whetten Ehninger's 1860 harvest landscape at the Smithsonian American Art Museum.
about: Golden light lies over trees and fields, and soft clouds glow above them. John Whetten Ehninger painted the clear air and bright colors of harvest time. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says a scene of peace and plenty hit harder after the Civil War, when it could recall a golden day before cannon fire tore up the fields. The museum quotes a poem from Harper's Weekly that asks what calls back the past like pumpkin pie.

meta: Autumn twilight over a harbor in Siebe Johannes ten Cate's 1901 pastel The Grand Quai of Le Havre, Cleveland Museum of Art.
about: This pastel looks along the quay at Le Havre at dusk in autumn. The Cleveland Museum of Art says it carries the damp chill of that hour. Siebe Johannes ten Cate was born in Holland. Most of his career was in Paris. For a short time he shared a Montmartre apartment with Kees van Dongen, and he knew Vincent van Gogh too. He was known for harbors and cityscapes. Here the light is nearly gone.

meta: A snake crawling over memorial offerings in Hokusai's Memorial Anniversary, a print from One Hundred Ghost Tales, 1831 to 1832.
about: A snake slides over the things set out for a memorial service: a box of sweets, a spirit tablet with the dead person's Buddhist name, and a green leaf floating in a bowl of water. The snake stands for malice. Hokusai seems to have planned a hundred prints, but only five are known. The title comes from a game where people told scary stories at night and snuffed a candle after each one. The Art Institute of Chicago adds that the bright blue was new and cheap, though viewers then linked it with death.

meta: Whistler holding his palette in front of Japanese scrolls and Chinese porcelain in The Artist in His Studio, 1865 to 1866.
about: Whistler looks straight out at us with a palette and brush in hand. Behind him hang three Japanese scrolls, and Chinese porcelain sits on shelves to the left. He used thin layers of muted paint so the surface would look as flat as a Japanese woodblock print. The Art Institute of Chicago also sees Velázquez here, since Las Meninas has a painter who shows himself at his easel as well. Whistler, an American living in London, put himself at the center of that mix of East and West.

meta: Mount Fuji reflected in the still surface of Lake Misaka in Hokusai's 1832 color woodcut, held by the Library of Congress.
about: The still surface of Lake Misaka acts like a mirror, and Mount Fuji hangs upside down in it. Hokusai made this color woodcut in 1832. The Library of Congress describes it as a print of the lake's mirror surface with the reflection of the mountain. Look at where the real shoreline ends and the reflection begins.

meta: Govert Flinck's Landscape with an Obelisk, painted in 1638 and stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston in 1990.
about: Thieves took this small panel from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston on 18 March 1990, and nobody has seen it since. Govert Flinck painted the landscape with an obelisk in 1638, in oil on wood. It is about 54 by 71 centimetres. For a time it was thought to be a Rembrandt. A reward of 10 million dollars is still offered for its return.

meta: Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith Beheading Holofernes, painted around 1620 and now in the Uffizi, is her second version of the story.
about: Judith and her maid Abra pin Holofernes to his bed while she drives a sword into him, and blood arcs across the white sheets. Artemisia Gentileschi painted this version around 1620. It hangs in the Uffizi in Florence. An earlier take on the story, from about 1612, is in Naples. Wikipedia points out that the two women have their sleeves rolled up, as if the killing were a household chore.

meta: Flora, goddess of spring, sits in a grotto holding columbine in Francesco Melzi's painting from around 1520, now in the Hermitage.
about: Flora, the Roman goddess of spring and flowers, sits in a grotto among ferns and ivy. White jasmine lies in her lap and she holds a spray of columbine in her left hand. Francesco Melzi, a pupil of Leonardo da Vinci, painted her around 1520, using Leonardo's soft shading and his face type with downcast eyes. Marie de' Medici owned the picture in 1649. It has been in the Hermitage in St. Petersburg since 1850.

meta: A Brescian merchant kneels in the crowd as a relic of the True Cross is carried through St. Mark's Square: Gentile Bellini, about 1496.
about: In 1444 a merchant from Brescia named Jacopo de' Salis knelt as a relic of the True Cross was carried through Piazza San Marco in Venice. He was praying for his dying son, and the boy recovered. Gentile Bellini painted the scene about fifty years later, in tempera on canvas. It was one of nine large canvases for a Venetian brotherhood. The merchant is hard to find. He kneels in red robes, just right of the last two men holding the canopy.

meta: The Van Lennep family of Smyrna sit on a yellow divan in Antoine de Favray's 1769 family portrait, in the Rijksmuseum.
about: David George van Lennep and his wife Anna Maria Leidstar sit on a yellow divan in the middle of this family portrait. They belonged to the Levantine elite of Smyrna, today's Izmir in Turkey. The Rijksmuseum says these families were mostly Dutch in origin, but no longer spoke the language and had taken on Turkish customs and dress. At the far left stands Anna Maria's father, the textile merchant Justinus Leidstar. Antoine de Favray painted the group in 1769.

meta: Berthe Morisot sketches while her small daughter Julie peers over her shoulder, in the 1888 print known as The Drawing Lesson.
about: Berthe Morisot shows herself sketching while her little daughter Julie leans in to look over her shoulder. The Rijksmuseum describes Morisot as a prominent member of the Paris Impressionists. She chose subjects such as motherhood and home life, and so gave women's everyday contemporary lives a visible place in art. She made this print in 1888, and it is known as The Drawing Lesson.

meta: A rider passes a beggar with an outstretched arm on a country road in Jan Wijnants's 1655 hilly landscape, in the Rijksmuseum.
about: A rider trots along a country road through hilly ground and passes a beggar who holds out an arm to him. Trees and a long ridge fill the distance. Jan Wijnants painted the landscape in 1655, and it is in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. The museum's own description names only these few things, the rider, the beggar and the far trees and ridge, and so they are what to look for.

meta: A beheading draws a crowd on the Groene Zoodje in front of the Binnenhof: Bartholomeus Dolendo's print of the Court of Holland, about 1610.
about: In the middle of the print, a beheading takes place on the Groene Zoodje while onlookers gather around. On the right stand the Gevangenpoort, the other buildings of the Binnenhof and the Hofvijver pond. The Buitenhof lies on the left. Bartholomeus Willemsz. Dolendo shows the Court of Holland in The Hague as it looked around 1610. The print is in the Rijksmuseum.

meta: Fashionable Victorians play lawn tennis in John Lavery's The Tennis Party, shown at the Royal Academy in 1885 and now in Aberdeen.
about: Fashionable Victorians play lawn tennis in this painting by John Lavery, made when the game was still new. It hung at the Royal Academy in London in 1885. Three years later it won a gold medal at the Paris Salon, which Wikipedia calls his breakthrough as a major artist. Lavery was an Irish painter and one of the Glasgow Boys. The collector James Murray gave the picture to Aberdeen Art Gallery in 1926.

meta: Jacobus Harrewijn's 1709 plan of Valenciennes, from a bound set of plans of battles and cities in the War of the Spanish Succession.
about: This is a city plan of Valenciennes, dated 1709. It comes from a bound collection of plans of battles and cities that became famous during the War of the Spanish Succession. Jacobus Harrewijn made the print, and it is now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. The sheet shows the town as a military map, laid out for readers who followed the war from home.

meta: A commemorative sheet for 1 April 1872, marking 300 years since the Sea Beggars took Den Briel, in the Rijksmuseum.
about: Three hundred years after the Sea Beggars captured Den Briel on 1 April 1572, the Netherlands held a national celebration on the same date. This printed sheet by Amand was made to mark the day. It is called Dutch Independence, and it groups its scenes around a single theme. The Rijksmuseum keeps it in its print collection.

meta: Sheep shearers at work in a timber shed in Tom Roberts's 1890 painting Shearing the Rams, in the National Gallery of Victoria.
about: Sheep shearers bend over their work in a timber shed. The shed is modelled on one at Brocklesby, a big sheep station near Corowa in New South Wales, where Tom Roberts made around 70 or 80 sketches in 1888. He came back the next shearing season with his canvas. The picture, finished in 1890, is called Shearing the Rams. It now belongs to the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne.
